tagline: Hills and turns connect Lake Michigan’s dunes with working fishing shanties.
intro: M-22 makes a U-shaped journey along Lake Michigan and the West Arm of Grand Traverse Bay, with numerous hills and turns along the way. The highway passes through Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore and the tourist communities of Leland and Suttons Bay. The M-22 Pure Michigan Byway organization emphasizes recreation, natural resources and cultural history, with protection of the corridor’s rural character an ongoing community goal. On the peninsula, Lake Michigan and Grand Traverse Bay moderate the climate, allowing apple and cherry growing to flourish alongside its wine industry.

The M-22 number dates to Michigan’s original 1919 highway system. Later reroutings moved the Suttons Bay–Traverse City stretch closer to the water, and the last gravel section, between Leland and Northport, was paved in 1945. The Leelanau section joined a heritage route with M-109 and M-204 in 2002; the rest of M-22 received a separate byway designation in 2016.

From US-31 northeast of Manistee, head north past Portage Lake and Arcadia, through Elberta and Frankfort, then curve along Crystal Lake’s north shore. Continue through Empire, between Little and Big Glen lakes to Glen Arbor, then north to Leland and Northport. Turn south along the bay through Suttons Bay and Greilickville to Traverse City.

moments.title: Point Betsie Lighthouse
moments.text: Point Betsie’s cylindrical tower stands on a dune at the southern entrance to the Manitou Passage, north of Frankfort. Construction finished in 1858, and the light entered service during the 1859 shipping season. The tower is attached to the keeper’s house, with its gambrel roof. Automation in 1983 ended staffing at the last staffed lighthouse on Lake Michigan. The old Fresnel lens was removed in 1996, stored at Sleeping Bear Dunes and later returned to the lighthouse as a nonworking display. A fog-signal building and oil house also survive at the site, though the original foghorn apparatus is gone.
moments.notice: The cylindrical tower rises from a dune beside the keeper’s house and its gambrel roof.

moments.title: Sleeping Bear Dunes
moments.text: Sleeping Bear’s perched dunes are layers of windblown sand resting on deposits of glacial debris. The landscape formed during the last glacial period, and the dunes have gradually migrated east. The national lakeshore, established in 1970, protects forests, beaches and dune formations along Lake Michigan, as well as North and South Manitou islands. Its flatter southern section includes Platte Bay and the Platte River mouth; farther north are Empire Bluff, Pyramid Point and the Dune Climb. The main Dune Climb lies across from Glen Lake. M-22 runs inland between Little and Big Glen lakes; M-109 provides a separate route through the lakeshore toward Glen Haven.

moments.title: Fishtown
moments.text: Wood-clad fishing buildings line both sides of the Leland River, most built by fishermen before 1930. In the early twentieth century, enclosed boats and gasoline engines increased the scale of local fishing. Sea lampreys devastated whitefish and trout populations in the 1940s; commercial fishing continued as tourism and charter operations became more important. High water began repeatedly flooding shanties in 2019, intensifying in 2020. The Village Cheese shanty was the first moved, in January 2020, as Fishtown Preservation worked to raise, repair and stabilize the buildings. The riverfront remains home to a working fishery as well as a charter-fishing business.
moments.notice: Fishing shanties, smokehouses and docks occupy the river outlet.

practical: Sleeping Bear Dunes: Drivers visiting the Dune Climb need a National Park Service day or annual pass. (checked 2026-10-11)
